_is.name: _is
_is.doc:
Return if the given instance inherits from the spec via nominal
typing.  Use `specIs()` to check nominal typing between two types.
Also see `fits()` and `specFits()` to check via structural typing.

Note that dict values will only match the generic 'sys.Dict'
type.  Use `fits()` for structural type matching.

Examples:
is("hi", Str)       >>  true
is("hi", Dict)      >>  false
is({}, Dict)        >>  true
is({equip}, Equip)  >>  false
is(Str, Spec)       >>  true

_trap.name: _trap
_trap.doc:
Function for the '->' operator.  If the given value is a dict,
then get a value by name, or throw UnknownNameErr if name not mapped.
If the value is a Ref, then perform a checked 'readById', then perform
the name lookup.

The trap function maybe be accessed using the '->' shortcut operator:
dict->foo  >>>  dict.trap("foo")

See `docHaxall::AxonLang#getAndTrap`.

_trap.name: _trap

the name lookup.

The trap function maybe be accessed using the `->` shortcut operator:

dict->foo  >>>  dict.trap("foo")

See [docHaxall::AxonLang#get-and-trap-operators].

addCol.name: addCol
addCol.doc:
Add a column to a grid by mapping each row to a new cell value.
The 'col' parameter may be a simple String name or may be a
dictionary which must have a "name" tag (any other
tags become column meta-data).  The mapping function takes
'(row)' and returns the new cell values for the column.

Examples:
                                   
  readAll(site).addCol("areaMeters") s => s->area.to(1m²)

                                                 
  readAll(site).addCol({name:"areaMeters", dis:"Area Meters"}) s => s->area.to(1m²)

readAll(site).addCol({name:"areaMeters", dis:"Area Meters"}) s => s->area.to(1m²)

all.name: all
all.doc:
Return if all the items in a list, dict, or grid match the
given test function.  If the collection is empty, then return
true.

If working with a list, the function takes '(val)'
or '(val, index)' and returns true or false.

If working with a dict, the function takes '(val)'
or '(val, name)' and returns true or false.

If working with a grid, the function takes '(row)'
or '(row, index)' and returns true or false.

If working with a string, the function takes '(char)'
or '(char, index)' and returns true or false.

If working with a stream, then function takes '(val)'
and returns true or false.  See `docHaxall::Streams#all`.

Examples:
  [1, 3, 5].all v => v.isOdd  >>  true
  [1, 3, 6].all(isOdd)        >>  false

arcDigest.name: arcDigest
arcDigest.doc:
Format a grid of arc summary records for a [notification]`lib:notify`.
If 'since' parameter is a span, then all arcs and parts that have been
modified in that span are returned. Otherwise, if 'since' is a DateTime,
then all arcs and parts from that time until now are returned.

                                                                    
  readAll(arc).arcDigest(dateTime(today(), 0:00))

arcEdit.name: arcEdit
arcEdit.doc:
Commit a diff to an existing arc rec.  Orig must be an arc record.  If
part is non-null, then it is a dict with new part to add the arc. Return
new arc document as grid.  See `ext-arc::doc#axon`.

arcEditPart.name: arcEditPart
arcEditPart.doc:
Edit an existing part on a record. Orig must be an arc record.  The origPart
must be a dict with the current part which you can get from the `arcRead()` grid.
The partChanges must be a dict diff with the tags to modify.  Return new arc document
as grid.  This function requires current user to have "editPart" permission.
See `ext-arc::doc#axon`.

arcMove.name: arcMove
arcMove.doc:
Move an arc document to another project database based on arcOn ref
Return new arc document as grid.

arcNew.name: arcNew
arcNew.doc:
Create a new arc.  Return new arc document as grid.
See `ext-arc::doc#axon`.

arcNewPart.name: arcNewPart
arcNewPart.doc:
Add a new part to an arc record.  Orig must be an arc record and part
must be a dict with the new part tags.  Return new arc document as grid.
This function requires current user to have "newPart" permission.
See `ext-arc::doc#axon`.

arcRead.name: arcRead
arcRead.doc:
Return the encoding of an arc and all its parts as a grid.
This function inserts a synthetic 'arcProjStatus' tag into the
grid meta along with the arc record itself.  See `ext-arc::doc#axon`.

arcReadAllUnder.name: arcReadAllUnder
arcReadAllUnder.doc:
Read summary grid of arcs with an `arcOn` contained by the given parent.
For example given a site, this will return all arcs on the children
spaces, equip, and points via the siteRef.  This function only reads
from the local project.  The optional filter may be used to specify
additional filtering of the results.

Example:
                                     
  read(site).arcReadAllUnder

                                            
  read(site).arcReadAllUnder(workorder and workorderState=="open")

arcRemovePart.name: arcRemovePart
arcRemovePart.doc:
Remove an existing part on a record. Orig must be an arc record.  The origPart
must be a dict with the current part which you can get from the `arcRead()` grid.
Return new arc document as grid.  This function requires current user to
have "editPart" permission. See `ext-arc::doc#axon`.

arcbeamCall.name: arcbeamCall
arcbeamCall.doc:
Evaluate a platform specific operation on the remote node.

For SkySpark and Haxall nodes, this will remotely evaluate an Axon
function using the same semantics as the `call()` function.  The the
current local user is used on the remote node.

Niagara nodes support a specific set of calls discussed in
the [Niagara Arcbeam docs]`docAppNotes::NiagaraArcbeam#niagaraCalls`.
Note that Niagara nodes do **not** support Haystack ops.

Examples:
                
  arcbeamCall(@conn, "about")

arcbeamEval.name: arcbeamEval
arcbeamEval.doc:
Evaluate a platform specific expression on the remote node.

For SkySpark and Haxall nodes, this will remotely evaluate an Axon
expression.  The the current local user is used on the remote node.

Examples:
  arcbeamEval(@conn, "readAll(equip)")

arcbeamRead.name: arcbeamRead
arcbeamRead.doc:
Read a single record from remote node with filter and return as a dict.
If not found, then return null or raise UnknownRecErr based on checked flag.

Examples:
  arcbeamRead(@conn, ahu and equip)

arcbeamReadAll.name: arcbeamReadAll
arcbeamReadAll.doc:
Read a grid of records from remote node with a filter.

Supported options for all remote node types:
  - limit: Number for max number of results

Supported [Niagara Options]`docAppNotes::NiagaraArcbeam#niagaraOpts`

Examples:
  arcbeamReadAll(@conn, ahu and equip)
  arcbeamReadAll(@conn, ahu and equip, {limit:10})

arcbeamReadById.name: arcbeamReadById
arcbeamReadById.doc:
Read a record from the remote node by its unique id and return as dict.
If the record is not found, then return null or raise UnknownRecErr
based on checked flag.

Examples:
  arcbeamReadById(@conn, @xyx-123)

arcbeamReadByIds.name: arcbeamReadByIds
arcbeamReadByIds.doc:
Read a list of records from remote node by their identifiers.  Return a
grid where each  row of the grid maps to the respective id list (indexes
line up).  If  checked is true and any one of the ids cannot be resolved
then raise UnknownRecErr for first id not resolved.  If checked is false,
then each id not found has a row where every cell is null.

Examples:
  arcbeamReadByIds(@conn, [@abc-123, @xyx-123])

call.name: call
call.doc:
Reflectively call a function with the given arguments.  The func
may be a Str name or an expression that evaluates to a function.
Args is a positional list for each argument.  Examples:

  call("today")
  call("replace", ["hi there", "hi", "hello"])
  call("parseDate", ["2021-03-15"])
  call("parseDate", ["15-Mar-21", "DD-MMM-YY"])
  call(parseDate, ["15-Mar-21", "DD-MMM-YY"])
  call(parseDate(_, "DD-MMM-YY"), ["15-Mar-21"])

call.name: call
call.doc:

Args is a positional list for each argument.  Examples:

call("parseDate", ["15-Mar-21", "DD-MMM-YY"])
call(parseDate, ["15-Mar-21", "DD-MMM-YY"])
call(parseDate(_, "DD-MMM-YY"), ["15-Mar-21"])

call("parseDate", ["15-Mar-21", "DD-MMM-YY"])

callByName.name: callByName
callByName.doc:
Reflectively call a function with arguments by name.  The func
may be a Str name or an expression that evaluates to a function.
Args a dict with the arguments keyed by name.  Note that null might
indicate an actual null argument or a fallback to a default value.
So any arguments are null, the pass a value for argument. Examples:

callByName("parseDate", {val:"01-02-03", pattern:"DD-MM-YY"})
callByName(parseDate, {val:"01-02-03", pattern:"DD-MM-YY"})

*Note that parameter names might change between releases.*

choiceOf.name: choiceOf
choiceOf.doc:
Given a choice spec, return the most specific choice subtype
implemented by the instance.  If the instance implements zero or more
than one subtype of the choice, then return null or raise an exception
based on the checked flag.  The instance may be anything accepted
by the `toRec()` function.

Example:
  choiceOf({discharge, duct}, DuctSection)  >>  DischargeDuct
  choiceOf({hot, water}, Fluid)             >>  HotWater

clamp.name: clamp
clamp.doc:
Clamp the number val between the min and max.  If its less than min
then return min, if its greater than max return max, otherwise return
val itself.  The min and max must have matching units or be unitless.
The result is always in the same unit as val.

Examples:
  14.clamp(10, 20)     >>   14                           
  3.clamp(10, 20)      >>   10                       
  73.clamp(10, 20)     >>   20                       
  45°F.clamp(60, 80)   >>   60°F

commit.name: commit
commit.doc:
Commit one or more diffs to the folio database.
The argument may be one of the following:
  - result of `diff()`
  - list of `diff()` to commit multiple diffs at once
  - stream of `diff()`; see `docHaxall::Streams#commit`.

If one diff is passed, return the new record.  If a list
of diffs is passed return a list of new records.

This is a synchronous blocking call which will return
the new record or records as the result.

Examples:
                   
  newRec: commit(diff(null, {dis:"New Rec!"}, {add}))

                                         
  readAll(filter).toRecList.map(r => diff(r, {someTag})).commit

covAvg.name: covAvg
covAvg.doc:
Folding function for generating a time weighted average
on change-of-value histories (where `hisInterpolate` is "cov").
The average is calcualted by weighting each sample with
its ratio of duration in the the overall interval.  For
example given the following time/value pairs:

  00:00  10
  02:00  30
  12:00  70

If performing a 1day rollup with the data above, the point
had a value of 10 for 2 hours, a value of 30 for ten hours,
and a value of 70 for 12 hours (until end of day).  The
time weighted COV average would be 48.3:
  10 * (2/24) + 30 * (10/24) + 70 * (12/24)

If any value in the rollup interval is `na()`, then the
result is `na()`.

degreeDays.name: degreeDays
degreeDays.doc:
Given a `site` or `weather` record compute both the heating and cooling
degree-days for the given date range.  The dates can be any range supported
by the `hisRead` function.  The 'base' parameter specifies the balance point:
- if null then `degreeDaysBase` is used
- if a number is passed, then it is used as both the heating and
  cooling balance temp
- otherwise must be a dict with "heat" and "cool" tags to specify
  different balance temps

The 'opts' parameter is a Dict that supports the following tags:
  - forecast: set to marker to include forecast data when computing degree days

Degree days are calculated using the average `air` `temp` for each day:
   heatDegreeDays = heatBase - avg                            
   coolDegreeDays = avg - coolBase                            

The results are returned as a history grid with the following columns:
- ts: midnight of each day computed
- heat: heating degree days in °daysF or °daysC
- cool: cooling degree days in °daysF or °daysC

Any dates where no `air` `temp` data is available are computed as null
degree days.

Examples
  read(site).degreeDays(2010-10)
  read(site).degreeDays(2010-10, 68°F)
  read(site).degreeDays(pastMonth, {heat:17°C, cool:20°C})
  read(site).degreeDays(pastMonth, {heat:17°C, cool:20°C}, {forecast})

degreeDaysBase.name: degreeDaysBase
degreeDaysBase.doc:
Given a `site` or `weather` record, return the default balance point
temperature to use for `degreeDays`.  This function can return a single
number to use for both the heating and cooling balance point, or it can
return a dict with separate balance points using the tags "heat" and "cool".
The number(s) returned must have an explicit unit of either °C or °F.
The default implementation is 18°C or 65°F. Also see `isMetric`.

Examples:
  65°F                                           
  {heat:17°C, cool:19°C}

diff.name: diff
diff.doc:
Construct a modification "diff" used by `commit`.  The orig should
be the instance which was read from the database, or it may be null
only if the add flag is passed.  Any tags to add/set/remove should
be included in the changes dict.

The following flags are supported:
  - 'add': indicates diff is adding new record
  - 'remove': indicates diff is removing record (in general you
    should add `trash` tag instead of removing)
  - 'transient': indicate that this diff should not be flushed
    to persistent storage (it may or may not be persisted).
  - 'force': indicating that changes should be applied regardless
    of other concurrent changes which may be been applied after
    the orig version was read (use with caution!)

Examples:
                       
   diff(null, {dis:"New Rec", someMarker}, {add})

                                                          
   diff(null, {id:151bd3c5-6ce3cb21, dis:"New Rec"}, {add})

                                       
   diff(orig, {dis:"New Dis", -oldTag})

                                 
   diff(orig, {val:123}, {transient})

Construct a modification "diff" used by `commit`.  The orig should

The following flags are supported:
- 'add': indicates diff is adding new record
- 'remove': indicates diff is removing record (in general you
should add `trash` tag instead of removing)
- 'transient': indicate that this diff should not be flushed
to persistent storage (it may or may not be persisted).
- 'force': indicating that changes should be applied regardless
of other concurrent changes which may be been applied after
the orig version was read (use with caution!)

Examples:
// create new record
diff(null, {dis:"New Rec", someMarker}, {add})

// create new record with explicit id like Diff.makeAdd

// set/add dis tag and remove oldTag
diff(orig, {dis:"New Dis", -oldTag})

diff(orig, {val:123}, {transient})

discreteBoolPeriods.name: discreteBoolPeriods
discreteBoolPeriods.doc:
Fold timestamp/bool value pairs into an encoded Str of discrete minutely
intervals. This rollup is similar to `discretePeriods` with the same
Base64 encoding. There are two significant differences:
  1. This rollup supports NA data
  2. Instead of encoding offset/duration pairs, the encoding is
     offset/ordinal pairs. The ordinal values map as '{0: false, 1: true, 2: NA}'

Also see `parseDiscreteBoolPeriods` and `haystack::Etc.discretePeriods`.

discreteEnumPeriods.name: discreteEnumPeriods
discreteEnumPeriods.doc:
Fold timestamp/enum Str value pairs into an encoded Str of discrete
minutely intervals.  This rollup works very similar to `discretePeriods`
with the same Base64 encoding.  The difference is that instead of
offset/duration pairs, the encoding is offset/ordinal pairs.  The
ordinal values map the position of each string value in the point's
`enum` tag.  If a string value is not mapped by 'enum' then a value
of 0xff (255) is used for the ordinal. If a string value is NA, then a
value of 0xfff (4095) is used for the ordinal.

Also see `parseDiscreteEnumPeriods` and `haystack::Etc.discretePeriods`.

discretePeriods.name: discretePeriods
discretePeriods.doc:
Fold timestamp/bool value pairs into an encoded Str of discrete minutely
intervals.  The string encoding is based on 12-bit minutely
start/duration pairs.  Each 12-bit minute offset/duration is encoded
using two 6-bit ASCII characters encoded by the Base64 table.
Also see `parseDiscretePeriods` and `haystack::Etc.discretePeriods`.

Here is the Fantom code which decodes a string to iterate a
period where 'time' is offset in minutes from base timestamp
and 'dur' is duration of period in minutes (assuming a minutely
interval).

    static Void decodePeriod(Str str, |Int time, Int dur| f)
    {
      for (i := 0; i<str.size; i += 4)
      {
        time := fromBase64[str[i+0]].shiftl(6) + fromBase64[str[i+1]]
        dur  := fromBase64[str[i+2]].shiftl(6) + fromBase64[str[i+3]]
        f(time, dur)
      }
    }

                           
    static const Str toBase64 :=
      "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789+/"
    static const Int[] fromBase64
    static
    {
      list := Int[,].fill(0, 128)
      toBase64.each |ch, i| { list[ch] = i }
      fromBase64 = list
    }

Note: the encoding size of 12-bits limits representations to offsets
of 4095 minutes or roughly 2.8 days.  Using using rollup intervals
over 1day cannot be represented using this encoding and will be silently
truncated past 2.8 days.

energyBaselinePrevMonth.name: energyBaselinePrevMonth
energyBaselinePrevMonth.doc:
Generate a baseline his grid based on last month's data.
Data from exactly 28days ago is used to ensure alignment by weekday.

energyBaselinePrevYear.name: energyBaselinePrevYear
energyBaselinePrevYear.doc:
Generate a baseline his grid based on last year's data.
Data from exactly 364days ago is used to ensure alignment by weekday.

energyNormByArea.name: energyNormByArea
energyNormByArea.doc:
Given a his grid, normalize the values by area in m² or ft².  Each
value column must have a `siteRef` which references a site with
the `area` tag.

energyNormByDegreeDay.name: energyNormByDegreeDay
energyNormByDegreeDay.doc:

- `password`
- `firstName`
- `lastName`
- `email`
- `org`

Return new account id

energyStarCustomerList.name: energyStarCustomerList
energyStarCustomerList.doc:

with following columns:

energyStarHisPull.name: energyStarHisPull
energyStarHisPull.doc:
Pull energy star usage into the given mapped meter points history.
The proxies may be any set of points
accepted by [toRecList].

Each point is required:
- define [energyStarConnRef] tag for connector to use
- define [energyStarMeter] for which meter it is mapped to
- must be a point with historized consumption values
- point's site must define [energyStarSite] tag

The EnergyStar usage must provide daily values which are mapped
to midnight of the starting date.

energyStarHisPush.name: energyStarHisPush
energyStarHisPush.doc:
Push the daily rollup consumption of mapped meter points to
portfolio manager.  The proxies may be any set of points
accepted by [toRecList].

Each point is required:
- define [energyStarConnRef] tag for connector to use
- define [energyStarMeter] for which meter it is mapped to
- must be a point with historized consumption values
- point's site must define [energyStarSite] tag

If the range is null, then we perform a read using [energyStarUsageRead]
to find the last endDate written.  Then we assume a range of endDate+1day
to yesterday.  This guarantees that we are only pushing newer data to
portfolio manager.

The usage to push is calcualted by perform a daily rollup on the history
using the [sum] function:

read(proxy).hisRead(range).hisClip.hisRollup(sum, 1day)

energyStarMeterDelete.name: energyStarMeterDelete
energyStarMeterDelete.doc:

the energy star Portfolio Manager.

Any recs with matching `energyStarMeter` value also have have

energyStarMeterList.name: energyStarMeterList
energyStarMeterList.doc:

- `id`: energy star meter id str
- `dis`: display name of the meter
- `association`: meter/property association formatted
as "meter: representation" such as "energyMeter: Whole Property".

energyStarMeterPull.name: energyStarMeterPull
energyStarMeterPull.doc:
Create or update a local meter point record from a meter in Portfolio Manager.
If an existing rec has [energyStarMeter] tag then it is the point to update.
If the point has to be created, then it is always placed under the main
electrict meter queried by `elecMeter and siteMeter`.  Or if a main meter is
not found, one is automatically created.  The point many not have all its tags
automatically created, so check the record in the BuilderApp.
See [doc#meterMapping].

energyStarMeterPush.name: energyStarMeterPush
energyStarMeterPush.doc:
Create or update a meter in Portfolio Manager from a local meter point record.
If the rec has [energyStarMeter] tag then it is the meter id to update.
Otherwise create a new meter and add [energyStarMeter] tag to the site record.
See [doc#meterMapping].

energyStarMeterRead.name: energyStarMeterRead
energyStarMeterRead.doc:
Read the given meter and return as Dict.
See [doc#meterMapping].

energyStarOnsiteRenewableDetailWrite.name: energyStarOnsiteRenewableDetailWrite
energyStarOnsiteRenewableDetailWrite.doc:
Write onsite green power renewable details.
See [https://portfoliomanager.energystar.gov/webservices/home/api/meter/onsite/post]
for details on this API request.
- `meterId`: The meter id of the meter to write details for
- `detail`: A Dict containing the details to write. The structure of this
Dict must adhere to the 'onsiteRenewableDetail.xsd' schema specified by
the API in the link above. It is your responsibility to construct a details
that meets the semantic constraints of the api - this func does constraint
checking.

```fantom
detail: {currentAsOf: 2024-12-06, energyUsedOnsite: {recOwnership: "Owned"}, energyExportedToGrid: {recOwnership: "Owned"}}
energyStarOnsiteRenewableDetailWrite(conn, meterId, detail)
```

energyStarPing.name: energyStarPing
energyStarPing.doc:
Asynchronously ping energy star connector to verify connectivity

energyStarPropertyAssociationsPush.name: energyStarPropertyAssociationsPush
energyStarPropertyAssociationsPush.doc:
This function recreates the list of property/meter associations in
Energy Star.  The site must be an id or record for a site which has
been mapped to Energy Star with an [energyStarSite] tag.  Associations
are created for every meter point within the site which has been
mapped with the [energyStarMeter] tag.  All associations are currently
mapped as "Whole Property'.  See [doc#associations].

energyStarPropertyDelete.name: energyStarPropertyDelete
energyStarPropertyDelete.doc:

energyStarPropertyList.name: energyStarPropertyList
energyStarPropertyList.doc:

- `id`: energy star property id str
- `dis`: display name of the property

By default this returns the properties associated with the
connector's accountId.  However if the connector defines the

energyStarPropertyMetrics.name: energyStarPropertyMetrics
energyStarPropertyMetrics.doc:
Read a list of metrics for a specific property.  The month to be
should be passed as month literal `YYYY-MM` or any Date in that month.
The metrics to be read as passed as Dict or markers and returned as
a Dict with the resulting values.  If the metric is not available, then
it is not included in the resulting Dict.

For list of metrics to query see
[EnergyStar Docs](http://portfoliomanager.energystar.gov/webservices/home/api/reporting/propertyMetrics/get).

Example:

energyStarPropertyMetrics(conn, "123", 2013-01, {score})  >>>  {score: 67}

energyStarPropertyPull.name: energyStarPropertyPull
energyStarPropertyPull.doc:
Create or update a local site record from a property in Portfolio Manager.
If an existing rec has [energyStarSite] tag then it is the site to update.
Otherwise create a new site record.  Note if there is navigation recs
above the site level, then you must manually add the appropiate ref tags.
If creating a new record, not all the tags may be get automatically created,
so check the record in the BuilderApp.
See [doc#siteMapping].

energyStarPropertyPush.name: energyStarPropertyPush
energyStarPropertyPush.doc:
Create or update a property in Portfolio Manager from a local site record.
If the rec has [energyStarSite] tag then it is the property id to update.
Otherwise a new property is created under the connector's account
and the [energyStarSite] tag is added to the site record.
See [doc#siteMapping].

energyStarPropertyRead.doc:

energyStarUsageDelete.name: energyStarUsageDelete
energyStarUsageDelete.doc: Delete the given usage item from portfolio manager

energyStarUsageRead.name: energyStarUsageRead
energyStarUsageRead.doc:
Read consumption data for given meter.  Return grid with cols:
- id: Str identifier for the consumption data item
- startDate: first Date of consumption
- endDate: last Date of consumption
- usage: Number for usage of date range
- recownership (optional): If present, the Str REC ownership status.
- energyExportedOffSite (optional): If present, the Number for the
amount of energy exported off site.

It is expected for the EnergyStar web service to give us pages of
data from newest dates down to oldest dates.  We continue to read
pages of data until no data is left or we hit our limit for rows of
usage data.

energyStarUsageWrite.name: energyStarUsageWrite
energyStarUsageWrite.doc:
Write consumption data to portfolio manager for given meter.
The usage must be grid with cols:
- startDate: first Date of consumption
- endDate: last Date of consumption (or if missing, startDate is assumed)
- usage: Number for usage of date range
- cost: (optional) Number for cost of usage
- estimatedValue: (optional) Marker or Bool indicating if the value is estimated.

evalToFunc.name: evalToFunc
evalToFunc.doc:
Evalate an Axon string expression to a function.  Typically the
expression is just a function name, but it can be any expression
that evaluates to a function.  Raise an exception if the expression
does not evaluate to a function. Note this call does evalute the
given expression in the runtime, so it must be used with caution - never
use it with a string from a non-trusted origin.

Examples:
  evalToFunc("now").call
  evalToFunc("(x, y)=>x+y").call([3, 4])
  (evalToFunc("(x, y)=>x+y"))(3, 4)
  evalToFunc("""replace(_, "x", "_")""").call(["xyz"])

eventCreate.name: eventCreate
eventCreate.doc:
Asynchronously create a new event for the given target and return a future.
The target may be any value accepted by `toRecId()`.  The event must be a dict
the defines a 'ts' DateTime with a UTC timezone.  The event dict may not
contain the 'event' nor the 'targetRef' tag.

Example:
  read(equip).eventCreate({ts:nowUtc(), dis:"Interesting event"})

eventDelete.name: eventDelete
eventDelete.doc:
Asynchronously delete a batch of events and return a future.  The target
may be any value accepted by `toRecId()`.  If the span argument is
a DateTime then we delete the event (or events) with the exact timestamp (any
timezone may be used).  Or span may be anything accepted by `toSpan()` to
delete a range of whole dates.  An optional filter may be specified to only
delete events that match the filter.  If both a span and filter are passed
then we only delete if both match (using AND logic).  Passing null for both
span and filter deletes all events for the target.

Example:

                                                 
  eventDelete(rec, ts)

                                                            
  eventDelete(rec, ts, myEvent)

                                 
  eventDelete(rec, lastMonth)

                                            
  eventDelete(rec, lastMonth, level=="debug")

                          
  eventDelete(rec, null, null)

eventRead.name: eventRead
eventRead.doc:
Read all the events for the given list of targets and span.  Return
the result as a grid.  The targets may be any value accepted by `toRecIdList()`.
The span may be any value accepted by `toSpan()` or null to read all stored
events.

If the 'tz' option is specified it is used for the timezone for
all timestamps, otherwise results are returned using the timezone
of the span (or if null the current timezone).

Examples:
                                  
  read(equip).eventRead(null)

                                 
  eventRead(@xyz-123, today)

                                      
  readAll(equip).eventRead(thisWeek)

                                                    
  readAll(equip).eventRead(thisWeek, severity=="warn")

                                           
  readAll(equip).eventRead(thisWeek, null, {tz:"Chicago"})

filter.name: filter
filter.doc:
Apply a [filter]`docHaystack::Filters` expression to a collection
of dicts.  The collection value may be any of the following:
 - Grid: returns new grid with filtered rows
 - Dict[]: returns list of filtered dicts (nulls are filtered out)
 - Col[]: returns list of columns filtered by their meta
 - Stream: filters stream of Dicts - see `docHaxall::Streams#filter`

The filter parameter may one fo the following:
  - Axon expression which maps to a filter
  - Filter from `parseFilter()`
  - Filter from `parseSearch()`

Examples:
                             
  [{v:1}, {v:2}, {v:3}, {v:4}].filter(v >= 3)

                                                           
  readAll(equip).filter(meter)

                               
  read(ahu).toPoints.hisRead(yesterday).cols.filter(kind=="Bool")

                               
  readAllStream(equip).filter(siteMeter and elec and meter).collect

                        
  readAll(equip).filter(parseSearch("RTU-1"))

filter.name: filter
filter.doc:
Apply a [filter]`docHaystack::Filters` expression to a collection
of dicts.  The collection value may be any of the following:
- Grid: returns new grid with filtered rows
- Dict[]: returns list of filtered dicts (nulls are filtered out)
- Col[]: returns list of columns filtered by their meta
- Stream: filters stream of Dicts - see `docHaxall::Streams#filter`

The filter parameter may one fo the following:
- Axon expression which maps to a filter
- Filter from `parseFilter()`
- Filter from `parseSearch()`

Examples:
// apply to a list of dicts
[{v:1}, {v:2}, {v:3}, {v:4}].filter(v >= 3)

// apply to a grid and return new grid with matching rows
readAll(equip).filter(meter)

// apply to a list of columns
read(ahu).toPoints.hisRead(yesterday).cols.filter(kind=="Bool")

// apply to a stream of dicts
readAllStream(equip).filter(siteMeter and elec and meter).collect

// apply search filter
readAll(equip).filter(parseSearch("RTU-1"))

find.name: find
find.doc:
Find the first matching item in a list or grid by
applying the given filter function.  If no match
is found return null.

If working with a list, the filter should be a function
that takes '(val)' or '(val, index)'.  It should return
true to match and return the item.

If working with a dict, the filter should be a function
that takes '(val)' or '(val, name)'.  It should return
true to match and return the item.

If working with a grid, the filter function takes '(row)'
or '(row, index)' and returns true to match and return the row.

If working with a stream, the filter takes '(val)' and returns
true to match.  See `docHaxall::Streams#find`.

Examples:
                                          
  ["ape", "bat", "charlie", "dingo"].find(x => x.size > 3)

                          
  [10, 4, 3, 7].find(isOdd)

Examples:

findAll.name: findAll
findAll.doc:
Find all the items in a list, dict, or grid by applying
the given filter function.  Also see `find`.

If working with a list, the filter should be a function
that takes '(val)' or '(val, index)'.  It should return
true to keep the item.

If working with a dict, the filter should be a function
that takes '(val)' or '(val, name)'.  It should return
the true to keep the name/value pair.

If working with a grid, the filter function takes '(row)'
or '(row, index)' and returns true to keep the row.  The
resulting grid shares the original's grid meta and columns.

If working with a stream, the filter takes '(val)' and returns
true to match.  See `docHaxall::Streams#findAll`.

Examples:
                                             
  ["ape", "bat", "charlie", "dingo"].findAll(x => x.size > 3)

                      
  [0, 1, 2, 3, 4].findAll(isEven)

                                                       
  readAll(site).findAll(s => s->area > 10_000ft²)

findAll.doc:
Find all the items in a list, dict, or grid by applying
the given filter function.  Also see [find].

If working with a list, the filter should be a function
that takes `(val)` or `(val, index)`.  It should return
true to keep the item.

If working with a dict, the filter should be a function
that takes `(val)` or `(val, name)`.  It should return
the true to keep the name/value pair.

If working with a grid, the filter function takes `(row)`
or `(row, index)` and returns true to keep the row.  The
resulting grid shares the original's grid meta and columns.

If working with a stream, the filter takes `(val)` and returns
true to match.  See [docHaxall::Streams#findall].

Examples:

// find all the strings longer than 3 chars
["ape", "bat", "charlie", "dingo"].findAll(x => x.size > 3)

// find even numbers
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4].findAll(isEven)

// find all the sites greater than 10,000ft from grid
readAll(site).findAll(s => s->area > 10_000ft²)

fitLinearRegression.name: fitLinearRegression
fitLinearRegression.doc:
Given a grid of x, y coordinates compute the best fit linear
regression equation using the ordinary least squares method.
The first column of the grid is used for 'x' and the second
column is 'y'.  Any rows without a Number for both x and y
are skipped.  Any special Numbers (infinity/NaN) are skipped.

Options:
  - 'x': column name to use for x if not first column
  - 'y': column name to use for y if not second column

The resulting linear equation is:

  yᵢ = mxᵢ + b

The equation is returned as a dictionary with these keys:
  - 'm': slope of the best fit regression line
  - 'b': intercept of the best fit regression line
  - 'r2':  R² coefficient of determination as a number between
    1.0 (perfect correlation) and 0.0 (no correlation)
  - 'xmin': minimum value of x variable in sample data
  - 'xmax': maximum value of x variable in sample data
  - 'ymin': minimum value of y variable in sample data
  - 'ymax': maximum value of y variable in sample data

Also see `matrixFitLinearRegression` to compute a multiple linear
regression.

Example:
  data: [{x:1, y:2},
         {x:2, y:4},
         {x:4, y:4},
         {x:6, y:5}].toGrid
   fitLinearRegression(data)

   >>> {m:0.4915, b: 2.1525, r2: 0.7502}

fits.name: fits
fits.doc:
Return if the given instance fits the spec via structural typing.
Use `specFits()` to check structural typing between two types.
Also see `is()` and `specIs()` to check via nominal typing.  Use
`fitsExplain()` to explain why fits returns true or false.

If the val is a Dict, then the default behavior is to only check
the dict's tags against the given spec.  In this mode all spec query
slots are ignored.  Pass the '{graph}' option to also check
queries to validate the graph of entities.  For example, the graph
option can be used with equip specs to validate required points.


Options:
  - 'graph': marker to also check graph of references such as required points
  - 'ignoreRefs': marker to not validate if refs exist or match target spec

Examples:
   fits("foo", Str)               >>  true
   fits(123, Str)                 >>  false
   fits(equipRec, Equip)          >>  true
   fits(equipRec, Site)           >>  false
   fits(vav, MyVavSpec)           >> validate tags only
   fits(vav, MyVavSpec, {graph})  >> validate tags and required points

fitsExplain.name: fitsExplain
fitsExplain.doc:
Return grid which explains how data fits the given spec.  This
function takes one or more recs and returns a grid.  For each rec
zero or more rows are returned with an error why the rec does not
fit the given type.  If a rec does fit the type, then zero rows are
returned for that record.

If you pass null for the spec, then each record is fit against
its declared 'spec' tag.  If a given rec is missing a 'spec' tag
then it is reported an error.

See `fits()` for list of options.

Example:
                                   
   readAll(vav and hotWaterHeating).fitsExplain(G36ReheatVav)

                                                               
   readAll(vav and hotWaterHeating).fitsExplain(G36ReheatVav, {graph})

argument can be anything accepted by `toRecList()`.  Specs must be a

all the non-abstract [types]`specs()` currently in scope.  Only the most

  - num: number of matches
  - specs: list of Spec for all matching specs

fold.name: fold
fold.doc:
Fold a list or stream into a single value using given folding function.
The folding function signature must be '(val, acc)' where val is the items
being folded, and acc is an accumulator used to maintain
state between iterations.  Lifecycle of a fold:
  1. Call 'fn(foldStart, null)', return initial accumulator state
  2. Call 'fn(item, acc)' for every item, return new accumulator state
  3. Call 'fn(foldEnd, acc)' return final result

See `docHaxall::Streams#fold` for streaming details.

The fold will short-circuit and halt immediately if the folding
function returns `na()` for the accumulator state. The result of
the fold is `na()` in this case.  A folding function should document
its behavior when a collection contains `na()`.

Built-in folding functions include:
  - `count()`
  - `sum()`
  - `avg()`
  - `min()`
  - `max()`
  - `mean()`
  - `median()`
  - `rootMeanSquareErr()`
  - `meanBiasErr()`
  - `standardDeviation()`

Examples:
  [1, 2, 3, 4].fold(max)                                 
  [1, 2, 3, 4].fold(avg)                                     
  [1, 2, na(), 3].fold(sum)           

Example of writing your own custom fold function that
used start/end values and has support for na():
   average: (val, acc) => do
     if (val == foldStart()) return {sum:0, count:0}
     if (val == foldEnd()) return acc->sum / acc->count
     if (val == na()) return na()
     return {sum: acc->sum + val, count: acc->count + 1}
   end
Also see `reduce()` which is easier to use if doing your
own simple rollup computation.

foldCols.name: foldCols
foldCols.doc:
Fold a set of columns in each row into a new folded column
and return a new grid.  The columns to fold are selected by the
'colSelector' function and removed from the result.  The selector
may be a list of string names or a function which takes a Col
and returns true to select it.  The folding function uses same
semantics as `fold`.


Example:
                                                    
  a    b    c
  ---  ---  ---
  1    10   100
  2    20   200

                                                           
  g.foldCols(["b", "c"], "bc", sum)

                      
  a    bc
  ---  ---
  1    110
  2    220

                                                            
  colSel: col => col.name == "b" or col.name == "c"
  g.foldCols(colSel, "bc", sum)

foldCols.name: foldCols

may be a list of string names or a function which takes a Col
and returns true to select it.  The folding function uses same
semantics as `fold`.


Example:
// consider grid 'g' with the following structure:
a    b    c
---  ---  ---
1    10   100
2    20   200

// foldCols, add b and c together to create new bc column
g.foldCols(["b", "c"], "bc", sum)

// yields this grid:
a    bc
---  ---
1    110
2    220

// we could also replace list of col names with a function
colSel: col => col.name == "b" or col.name == "c"
g.foldCols(colSel, "bc", sum)

haystackEval.name: haystackEval
haystackEval.doc:
Evaluate an Axon expression in a remote server over
a haystack connector.  The remote server must be a SkySpark
server which supports the "eval" REST op with an Axon
expression.  This function blocks while the network request is
made.  The result is always returned as a Grid using the same
rules as `haystack::Etc.toGrid`.

The expression to evaluate in the remote server may capture
variables from the local scope.  If these variables are atomic types,
then they are captured as defined by local scope and serialized
to the remote server.  Pass '{debug}' for opts to dump to stdout
the actual expr with serialized scope.

Options:
  - 'debug': dumps full expr with seralized scope to stdout
  - 'evalTimeout': duration number to override remote project's
    default [evalTimeout]`docSkySpark::Tuning#folio`

Examples:
  read(haystackConn).haystackEval(3 + 4)
  read(haystackConn).haystackEval(readAll(site))
  read(haystackConn).haystackEval(readAll(kw).hisRead(yesterday))

identifiers.  Return a grid where each row of the grid maps to the
respective id list (indexes line up).  If checked is true and any one
of the ids cannot be resolved then raise UnknownRecErr for first id not
resolved.  If checked is false, then each id not found has a row
where every cell is null.  Also see `haystack::Client.readByIds`.

haystackReadByIds.name: haystackReadByIds
haystackReadByIds.doc:
Perform Haystack HTTP API call to read a list of records by their
identifiers.  Return a grid where each row of the grid maps to the
respective id list (indexes line up).  If checked is true and any one
of the ids cannot be resolved then raise UnknownRecErr for first id not
resolved.  If checked is false, then each id not found has a row
where every cell is null.  Also see `haystack::Client.readByIds`.

haystackReadByIds.name: haystackReadByIds
haystackReadByIds.doc:
Perform Haystack HTTP API call to read a list of records by their
identifiers.  Return a grid where each row of the grid maps to the
respective id list (indexes line up).  If checked is true and any one
of the ids cannot be resolved then raise UnknownRecErr for first id not
resolved.  If checked is false, then each id not found has a row
where every cell is null.  Also see [haystack::Client.readByIds].

help.name: help
help.doc:
Print help summary or help on a specific command.
Examples:
help()        // print summary
help(using)   // print help for the using function

helpAll.name: helpAll
helpAll.doc: Print help summary of every function

hisClear.name: hisClear
hisClear.doc:
Clear the history items in the given range.  This function has
similiar semantics as `hisRemove()` except:
  - it supports multiple history records as a target
  - it only supports a single span or null

WARNING: once the data is cleared, there is **NO** recovery!!!

The hisArg contains the list of histories to query using any
value supported by the `toRecList` function.  See `hisRead`.

The span can be any non-null span accepted by `hisRead` or null.
A null value will delete all the history data for each point.
Unlike `hisRemove()` the span cannot be a list nor a single DateTime.

The result of this function is unspecified and may change.

hisClip.name: hisClip
hisClip.doc:
Remove the rows with leading/trailing timestamps from the
actual query range.  The query range is defined as inclusive
of 'meta.hisStart' and exclusive of 'meta.hisEnd'.  These
meta tags are derived from the dates range passed to the `hisRead`
function.

Example:
  hisRead(points, dates).hisClip

hisCollectReset.name: hisCollectReset
hisCollectReset.doc: Force history collector to recreate its watch

hisCollectReset.name: hisCollectReset
hisCollectReset.doc: Force history collector to recreate its watch

hisCollectWriteAll.name: hisCollectWriteAll
hisCollectWriteAll.doc:
Write all hisCollect items buffered in memory to the historian.
Block until complete or until timeout exceeded.

hisCollectWriteAll.name: hisCollectWriteAll
hisCollectWriteAll.doc:
Write all hisCollect items buffered in memory to the historian.
Block until complete or until timeout exceeded.

hisCollectWriteAll.name: hisCollectWriteAll
hisCollectWriteAll.doc:
Write all hisCollect items buffered in memory to the historian.
Block until complete or until timeout exceeded.

hisCompare.name: hisCompare
hisCompare.doc:
Compare a history query against an alternate set of dates.
This function takes the result of a history query, potentially
with transforms using `hisMap`, `hisRollup`, etc.

The original query is re-run againts the new starting dates
using the same duration as the original query.  For example if
the original duration was over 7days, then comparison queries
will also be 7days.

The comparison values are are added as columns "vNxM" where "N"
represents the originals "v0", "v1" columns and "M" represents
the comparison dates.  The timestamps are aligned on the hour
of the day based on the original query.

The dates may be one of the following:
  - Date: convenience for '[date]'
  - Date[]: list of starting dates
  - DateSpan: convenience for month with starting
    date is aligned to base query by weekdays
  - DateSpan[]: convenience for list months aligned by weekday
  - Int: convenience for 1st of year aligned by weekday
  - Int[]: convenience for list of 1st of years
  - Func: function which evaluates to one of the above supported types

hisCuSum.name: hisCuSum
hisCuSum.doc:
Calculate a simplified cumulative sum (CuSum) for the given history
grid. The 'v0' column is treated as the "actual" value, and the 'v1'
column is treated as the "target" value.

Example:

                               
  ts, v0, v1
  00:00, 100 kWh, 150 kWh
  01:00, 175 kWh, 100 kWh
  02:00,  50 kWh, 100 kWh

                   
  hisCuSum(src)

                   
  ts, v0
  00:00, -50 kWh
  01:00,  25 kWh
  02:00, -25 kWh

NOTE: this function is subject to change

hisDailyProfile.name: hisDailyProfile
hisDailyProfile.doc:
Perform a rollup by time slice to produce a single 24-hour
profile of the data. The input must be a history grid with
a 'ts' DateTime column and timestamps spread across a uniform
interval (typically result of `hisRollup`).  The result
replaces 'ts' with a 'time' column for each unique time-slice.

For example, let's consider we wish to generate an average
daily profile of our energy use in Jan of 2010.  Assuming
have 15-min demand data we would start with this rollup:

  hisRead(pt, 2010-01).hisRollup(max, 1hr)

This produces a grid with one row for each hour of the month.
The values of the grid are the peak demand within each hour
window (using the `max` function).  Now let's say we wish
to average the entire month to get average peak for each
one hour time slice:

  hisRead(pt, 2010-01).hisRollup(max, 1hr).hisDailyProfile(avg)

The resulting grid will have 24 rows with the average of each
time-slice:

  time    val
  -----   ----
  00:00   avg(01-Jan 00:00, 02-Jan 00:00, ... 31-Jan 00:00)
  01:00   avg(01-Jan 01:00, 02-Jan 01:00, ... 31-Jan 01:00)
  ....
  23:00   avg(01-Jan 23:00, 02-Jan 23:00, ... 31-Jan 23:00)

hisDurProfile.name: hisDurProfile
hisDurProfile.doc:
Compute a "load duration" curve.  The input must be a history
grid with a 'ts' DateTime column and all the values must be
numbers with a uniform unit.  The result is a grid shaped as
follows:

   bucket   v0            v1
   ------   -----------   ----------
     a      dur v0 >= a   dur v1 >= a  ...
     b      dur v0 >= b   dur v1 >= b  ...
   ....

The function creates 100 buckets based on the min/max range
of all the values contained by the input grid.  The 'ts' column
is replaced by a 'bucket' column which defines 100 discrete
"buckets" of the value range.  The input's value columns and meta
remain unchanged.  The cells of the value columns define the number
of hours the value is greater than or equal to the bucket value.

By default gaps in the data over 1hour are ignored.  If
the 'hisInterval' grid.meta is specified and it is over 1hr,
then it is used as the gap threshold.

hisFindAll.name: hisFindAll
hisFindAll.doc:
Perform a filter transformation on a history grid.  The
filter function takes '(val, ts, his)' and returns
true or false.

By default, empty columns will be removed. To keep empty columns you may
do one of the following:
  1. pass the 'hisKeepEmptyCols' option to `hisRead`
  1. add the 'hisKeepEmptyCols' marker tag to the history grid meta
     using `addMeta`

hisFindInPeriods.name: hisFindInPeriods
hisFindInPeriods.doc:
Perform filter transformation on a history grid by finding
all rows which have a timestamp within the given periods.  The
periods grid must be in the standard format for history periods
where first column is 'ts' timestamp and second column is
values measured in hours.

By default, empty columns will be removed. To keep empty columns you may
do one of the following:
  1. pass the 'hisKeepEmptyCols' option to `hisRead`
  1. add the 'hisKeepEmptyCols' marker tag to the history grid meta
     using `addMeta`

hisFindPeaks.name: hisFindPeaks
hisFindPeaks.doc:
Filter a history grid so that only numeric samples that represent
a peak are returned.  A peak is defined as a timestamp/value
pair where both the previous and next value is smaller.  Non-numeric
columns are filtered out.  If the source grid has multiple
numeric value columns, then non-peak cells are set to null.
Also see `hisFindTroughs`.

hisFindPeriods.name: hisFindPeriods
hisFindPeriods.doc:
Find all the periods of time when 'fn' returns true for a history
grid.  The filter func takes '(val, ts, his)' and returns true
or false. This function only works on data up to the current time; it does
not work with future data.

By default, empty columns will be removed. To keep empty columns you may
do one of the following:
  1. pass the 'hisKeepEmptyCols' option to `hisRead`
  1. add the 'hisKeepEmptyCols' marker tag to the history grid meta
     using `addMeta`

hisFindSlicePeriods.name: hisFindSlicePeriods
hisFindSlicePeriods.doc:
Given a source history grid and a grid of windows, compute the
periods of all the slices matched by given function. For each window
in the widows grid, the `hisSlice` is computed and passed
to the function as '(grid)'.  If the function returns true the
window is added to the resulting periods.  Adjacent or overlapping
windows are coalesced together in the period results.

See [Windows and Slices]`ext-hisKit::doc#windowsAndSlices`

hisFindTroughs.name: hisFindTroughs
hisFindTroughs.doc:
Filter a history grid so that only numeric samples that represent
a trough are returned.  A trough is defined as a timestamp/value
pair where both the previous and next value is larger.  Non-numeric
columns are implicitly filtered out.  If the source grid has multiple
numeric value columns, then non-trough cells are set to null.
Also see `hisFindPeaks`.

hisFlatten.name: hisFlatten
hisFlatten.doc:
Perform a transformation on the history to flatten out ts/val
pairs into new rows.  The mapping function takes '(val, ts, his)'
and returns a dict for the flattened row.  Given a grid with 'n'
val colums, and 'm' rows, the resulting grid has 'n x m' rows.  The
resulting columns are determined by the dicts returned from the
mapping func.

hisFoldCols.name: hisFoldCols
hisFoldCols.doc:
Given a history grid, fold all the value columns (every
column* except "ts") into a single "v0" column.

Examples:
  readAll(kw).hisRead(lastWeek).hisFoldCols(sum)

hisInWindows.name: hisInWindows
hisInWindows.doc:
Return true or false if the given timestamp is inside at least
one of the given windows.  The 'ts' parameter may be either a
DateTime or a Dict/Row with a 'ts' tag/column.  The 'windows'
parameter must be a grid of timestamp/duration rows. Windows
are start-inclusive and end-exclusive for timestamp comparisons.

See [Windows and Slices]`ext-hisKit::doc#windowsAndSlices`

Example:
                                                 
  hisRead(points, dates).findAll(row => hisInWindows(row, windows))

hisInterpolate.name: hisInterpolate
hisInterpolate.doc:
Interpolate all the null value cells for each timestamp.
See [Interpolation]`ext-hisKit::doc#interpolation` for details.

hisJoin.name: hisJoin
hisJoin.doc:
Given a list of history grids, join them by the 'ts' timestamp
column.  This function automatically renames columns to ensure
each column in result has a unique name.  Grid meta is merged in
order of grids parameter, however all "hisX" meta tags are stripped,
and new 'hisStart' and 'hisEnd' are computed based on a merged range.

The following options are supported:
 - 'tz': specifies the timezone for the 'ts' column for the join.
   If omitted, and all the histories have the same timezone then
   that is the timezone used by 'ts'.  Otherwise histories are joined
   by relative time of day using "Etc/Rel".  If an explicit timezone
   other than "Etc/Rel" is specified, then timestamps are joined by
   absolute time.

Example:
  a: hisRead(pointA, dates)
  b: hisRead(pointB, dates)
  hisJoin([a, b])

hisMap.name: hisMap
hisMap.doc:
Perform a map transformation on the history value cells.  The
mapping function takes '(val, ts, his)' and returns new vals.
The src must be a history grid.

By default, empty columns will be removed. To keep empty columns you may
do one of the following:
  1. pass the 'hisKeepEmptyCols' option to `hisRead`
  1. add the 'hisKeepEmptyCols' marker tag to the history grid meta
     using `addMeta`

hisMapSlices.name: hisMapSlices
hisMapSlices.doc:
Given a source history grid and a grid of windows, compute the
mapping of each slice.  For each window in the widows grid,
the `hisSlice` is computed and passed to the function as '(grid)'.
The function must return a dict for resulting row or null to
skip mapping that window/slice.

See [Windows and Slices]`ext-hisKit::doc#windowsAndSlices`

hisPeriodIntersection.name: hisPeriodIntersection
hisPeriodIntersection.doc:
Find the intersection of two or more historical periods. The 'periods'
parameter may be:
  - Grid: a single grid where the first column is a "ts" column,
  and all remaining columns are named anything and contain period values.
  - Grid?[]: a list of grids where each grid has the format described above

All input grids must be [normalized]`hisPeriodNormalize()`

The resulting grid has "ts" and "v0" column, where "v0" is duration in hours.

Example:
                                          
  hisPeriodIntersection([a, b])

hisPeriodMatrix.name: hisPeriodMatrix
hisPeriodMatrix.doc:
Get a grid which defines the "matrix" of unique combinations of all the
periods merged together. The 'periods' parameter may be:
  - Grid: a single grid where the first column is a "ts" column,
  and all remaining columns are named anything and contain period values.
  - Grid?[]: a list of grids where each grid has the format described above,

All input grids must be [normalized]`hisPeriodNormalize()`

The result is returned as a grid with these columns:
  - 'ts': starting timestamp of each unique period
  - 'dur': duration in hours of each unique period
  - 'numTrue': number of input periods "on" during period
  - 'v{i}': true of false indicating if input was "on" during that period

Example, lets assume we have three unit runtime periods a, b, and c:
                                                 
  hisPeriodMatrix([a, b, c]).findAll r => r->numTrue == 0

                                                
  hisPeriodMatrix([a, b, c]).findAll r => r->numTrue == 3

                                                        
  hisPeriodMatrix([a, b, c]).findAll r => r->v0 and r->v1 and not r->v2

hisPeriodNormalize.name: hisPeriodNormalize
hisPeriodNormalize.doc:
Given a grid of historical periods, merge any overlapping periods to result
in a "normalized" [his period grid]`ext-his::doc#hisPeriodGrid`.

Examples:
                  
  02:00 1hr
  02:30 3hr

  hisPeriodNormalize(src)
  02:00 3.5hr

hisPeriodShift.name: hisPeriodShift
hisPeriodShift.doc:
Given of a grid of historical periods, shift the starting and ending
timestamps by an offset.  The input grids must have a "ts" timestamp
column and value columns of duration.  The 'startShift' specifies a
positive or negative shift of the starting timestamp of each period.
The 'endShift' indicates the amount to add/remove to each period
duration (shifting the implied end timestamp).  If the shift results
a negative duration, then that period it is removed.  If the shift
creates overlapping periods, then they are merged.

Examples:
                  
  02:00  1hr
  08:00  4hr
  13:00  5hr

                                                             
                                                  
  hisPeriodShift(src, 1hr, -2hr)
  09:00  1hr
  14:00  2hr

                                                           
                                                            
  hisPeriodShift(src, 0hr, 3hr)
  02:00  4hr
  08:00  13hr

hisPeriodUnion.name: hisPeriodUnion
hisPeriodUnion.doc:
Find the union of two or more historical periods. The 'periods'
parameter may be:
  - Grid?: a single grid where the first column is a "ts" column,
  and all remaining columns are named anything and contain period values.
  - Grid?[]: a list of grids where each grid has the format described above,

All input grids must be [normalized]`hisPeriodNormalize()`

The resulting grid has "ts" and "v0" column, where "v0" is duration in hours.

Example:
                                              
  hisPeriodUnion([a, b, c])

hisRead.name: hisRead
hisRead.doc:
Query history for an arbitrary range.  The result is a grid with
a column called "ts", and multiple "v0", "v1", etc columns with
the values joined by timestamp.

The hisRefs contains the list of histories to query using any
value supported by the `toRecList` function:
  - Ref or Ref[] to his
  - Dict/Row or Dict[]/Row[] of his
  - Grid of his

Any records which don't support the 'his' tag are silently ignored.
If no records with the 'his' tag are specified then an exception is
thrown.

The dates specifies the start/ending times of the query:
  - if start is null, then we use oldest item
  - if end is null, then we use most recent item
  - if start is Date, then we use midnight of that day
  - if end is Date, then we use midnight of next after
  - otherwise start/end must be DateTimes

The following convenience values are also allowed for range:
  - Date: convenience for 'date..date'
  - null: convenience for 'null..null'
  - Int: if between 1900 and 2100 convenience for entire year
  - Fn: function is resolved to one of the above 'today' vs 'today()'

The result always includes the previous item immediately before
the range, and immediately after the range.  The leading/trailing
values are often needed to interpret the first/last values of
the result.  If leading/trailing values are not desired, then pipe
the result of this function to `hisClip`

The following options are supported:
 - 'limit': used to cap the number of records generated
   by the query. The default is 10,000.  You may use Remove.val
   to indicate no limit such as '{-limit}'.
 - 'tz': specifies the timezone for the 'ts' column used to join
   multiple histories.  If omitted, and all the histories have
   the same timezone then that is the timezone used by 'ts'.
   Otherwise histories are joined by relative time of day using
   "Etc/Rel".  If an explicit timezone other than "Etc/Rel" is
   specified, then timestamps are joined by absolute time.
 - 'hisTotalized': set to Remove.val to disable delta reads of
   of hisTotalized recs (reads raw values); in Axon you can
   specify this like '{-hisTotalized}'.
 - 'hisMode': set to Remove.val to force all reads to behave
   as though the hisMode tag was not set on the rec; in Axon
   you can specify this like '{-hisMode}'.
 - 'hisAppendNA': set to Remove.val to disable the append NA
   threshold on histories that have this tag.; in Axon you
   specify this like '{-hisAppendNA}'. See `hisAppendNA` for
   details.
 - 'hisFunc': set to Remove.val to disable the computed function
   for this point. Can only be used on
   [writable computed points]`ext-his::doc#hisFuncWritable`.  In Axon
   you can specify this like '{-hisFunc}'.
 - 'raw': set to Marker.val to disable all transformations
   of the history read; in Axon you can specify this like '{raw}'.
   This option is equivalent to '{-hisTotalized, -hisMode, -hisAppendNA, -hisFunc}'.
 - 'forecast': include [forecast items]`ext-his::doc#forecast`
 - 'forecastOnly': include only [forecast items]`ext-his::doc#forecast`

Note that the query limit is applied to the pipeline, not the
raw 'hisRead'.  So if 'hisRead' is piped directly to a 'hisRollup',
the limit will apply to the number of rollup rows, not raw
rows.  Unless configured in opts, the default limit is 10,000.
This value may be overridden by applying the 'hisLimit' tag
on the HisExt record.  If the limit is hit and more data is
available, then grid meta has the 'limit' and 'more' tags defined.

Also see `ext-his::doc#queries`.

hisRemove.name: hisRemove
hisRemove.doc:
Remove items from a history using a timestamp or timestamp range.
This function blocks until the remove is complete.

WARNING: once the data is removed, there is **NO** recovery!!!

The hisRec supports anything accepted by `toRec`.  Note this
function only works on one record at a time.

The spans argument can be any non-null span accepted by `hisRead` or
a list of such spans.  If a single DateTime is used then just
that item is removed, otherwise any items within the span's
inclusive start time and exclusive end time are removed.  Note that
timestamps are normalized according to the record's `hisTsPrecision`.

This function is best used for fine grained removal.  Also see
the `hisClear()` function for removing multiple points or the
entire history.

The result of this function is unspecified and may change.

Examples:
  hisRemove(pt, ts)                                   
  hisRemove(pt, startTs..endTs)                         
  hisRemove(pt, [ts1, ts2])

hisRewrite.name: hisRewrite
hisRewrite.doc:
Rewrite every item of a history using the given transformation
function.  This function will automatically update the 'kind',
'tz', and 'unit' tag if the mapping function returns a new timezone,
new value type, or new unit.  The mapping function takes '(val, ts, his)'
and returns new items as tuple list of '[ts, val]' or null to omit
a specific writing item.

CAUTION: This function will read and rewrite every item and
there is no undo, so use it with care!

The hisArg contains the list of histories to rewrite using any
value supported by the `toRecList` function.  See `hisRead`.

Return a grid with a row for each history converted.  The following
columns are included:
  - id: of the history record
  - dis: dis string of the history record
  - numRewritten: number of history items rewritten

Side effects:
  - rewrites every history item
  - clears context read cache

Examples:
                                    
  hisRewrite(hisId) (val, ts) => [ts.toTimeZone("New_York"), val]

                                        
  hisRewrite(hisId) (val, ts) => [ts, val != 0]

                  
  hisRewrite(hisId) (val, ts) => [ts, val.to("kW")]

hisRollup.name: hisRollup
hisRollup.doc:
Roll up a history grid over discrete intervals of time with
the given fold function.  The src must be a history grid created
from `hisRead` or some transformation of it.

Rollups are inclusive of start and exclusive of end times.
For example a daily rollup includes midnight of the current day,
but excludes midnight of the next day. All the items found within
the interval are passed to the folding function to compute a
timestamp/val pair with each timestamp aligned to the start of the
interval.  Use the string "*" to rollup the entire grid as one
big interval.

For example a rollup interval of 1day over a one year range
would calculate 365 (or 366 if leap year) items with the
start time being midnight of each day. Interval rules:
 - Less 1day: use absolute time, aligned off start (example 1hr)
 - 1day: daily rollup, aligned off midnight
 - 1wk: weekly rollup, aligned off midnight on Sunday
 - 1mo: monthly rollup, aligned off midnight on 1st of month
 - 3mo: quarterly rollup, aligned off midnight on 1st of 3 month intervals
 - 1yr: yearly rollup, aligned off midnight Jan 1st
 - Anything else is an error

See 'core::fold' for how folding functions work.  History rollups
also support rollup functions with arity of 3 '(val, ts, acc)'.

This function will work with [forecast data]`ext-his::doc#forecast` provided
one of the following is true:
 1. You did the initial `hisRead()` with the '{forecast}' option
 1. The column metadata for the value has a `hisEnd` in the future
 1. The data comes from a computed point (`hisFunc`)
 1. The data does not come from a demo database

hisRollupAuto.name: hisRollupAuto
hisRollupAuto.doc:
Automatically chooses the best rollup interval and the best rollup
fold function for each history.

If null is passed for the interval, then the following automatic
selection is made:
  - less 2days: Check each history rec to see if any specify the `hisRollupAutoMinInterval`
    tag and take the *maximum* value. Otherwise, no rollup is applied and the raw
    history grid is returned.
  - one week: 10min interval
  - one month: 1hour interval
  - over one month: daily interval

The rollup function applied to each history is determined as follows:
  1. if foldFinder parameter is specified, it is called for each
     history to get fold function.  If it returns null we check next
     step
  2. if `hisRollupFunc` is defined on the history, then use it
  3. Select fold function based on kind:
     a. Bool: `discreteBoolPeriods`
     b. Number with `hisMode` of "cov": `covAvg`
     c. Number pick based on unit's quantity:
       - power: `max`
       - volume, energy: `sum`
       - default: `avg`
     d. Str with enum tag: `discreteEnumPeriods`
     e. fallback to `count`

If your history has no data or is a computed history, you should
explicitly specify the `kind` or `hisRollupFunc` to ensure a suitable
rollup is selected.

If a rollup is applied, then the following tags are automatically
applied to the resulting grid:
  - 'hisRollupInterval': applied to grid.meta interval used for the rollup
  - 'hisRollup': applied to col.meta of each value column (such as "avg")
  - 'hisRollupDis': applied to col.meta for each rollup, if all the columns
    have the same rollup, then it is applied to grid.meta also

Examples:
                       
  src.hisRead(pastWeek).hisRollupAuto

                       
  src.hisRead(pastMonth).hisRollupAuto

                            
  src.hisRead(pastMonth).hisRollupAuto(1day)

                                                   
  src.hisRead(pastMonth).hisRollupAuto(null, his => max)

hisRollups.name: hisRollups
hisRollups.doc:
Perform a series of rollups over discrete intervals.  This
function works just like `hisRollup`, but takes a list of
folding functions.  Instead of a single value per input history,
there are a series of columns for each folding function.
For example if the input has a 'v0' and 'v1' column and the
folding functions are '[min, max]', then the resulting grid
will have 'v0_min', 'v0_max', 'v1_min', and 'v1_max'.

hisSlice.name: hisSlice
hisSlice.doc:
Slice a source history grid by a single time window.  Slices
only include items from the source grid which are inclusive of
the window time range.  The starting and ending rows are always
the time boundaries of window with the values interpolated (or
null if they cannot be interpolated).

Example:

                               
  ts, v0
  00:00, 20, true
  01:00, 30, false
  02:00, 40, null
  03:00, 50, true
  04:00, 60, false

                   
  hisSlice(src, dateTime(date, 1:30), 2hr)

                   
  ts, val
  1:30, 35, false
  2:00, 40, null
  3:00, 50, true
  3:30, 55, true

Note in the example above that we added a row at beginning and at the
end for the window boundaries.  The values of these boundary
rows are interpolated from the original data.

See [Windows and Slices]`ext-hisKit::doc#windowsAndSlices`

hisSlidingWindows.name: hisSlidingWindows
hisSlidingWindows.doc:
Compute of grid of timestamp/duration windows.  The window start
times are defined by 'range' and 'step' parameter.  The window
duration is defined by 'dur' parameter.  The last window's end
timestamp is always before or equal to the range ending timestamp.

 - 'range': may be any date/datetime range supported by `hisRead` or
   may be a history grid itself in which case the hisStart/hisEnd
   grid meta tags are used as the range
 - 'dur': Number with duration unit, standard unit is hour
 - 'step': Number with duration unit, standard unit is hour

See [Windows and Slices]`ext-hisKit::doc#windowsAndSlices`

Example:

                                           
  hisSlidingWindows(2011-07-04, 1hr, 30min)

                   
  ts, v0

hisTransitionWindows.name: hisTransitionWindows
hisTransitionWindows.doc:
Compute a grid of timestamp/duration windows based on transitions
of a history grid.  The window duration is defined by the 'dur'
parameter.  The transitions are determined by the 'fn' parameter
which is a function of '(row, row)' which returns trues to create
a transition window.

The 'dur' parameter may be one of the following:
  Dur Value             Window
  ---------             -------
  Positive Number       ts .. ts+dur
  Negative Number       ts+dur .. ts
  Range of two Numbers  ts+dur.start .. ts+dur.end

In all cases above the numbers must have a duration unit (hour is
standard).  The timestamp uses is always the later of the rows being
compared.  Here are some examples assuming transition time of '2:00':

   15min          >>  2:00 to 2:15                   
   -15min         >>  1:45 to 2:00                    
   -20min..20min  >>  1:40 to 2:20                 
   -1hr..-30min   >>  1:00 to 1:30                             
    1hr..2hr      >>  3:00 to 4:00                            

Example:

                               
  ts, v0
  00:00, false
  08:00, true
  17:00, false
  19:00, true
  20:00, false

                                                        
                                             
  hisTransitionWindows(src, 30min) (a,b) => a->v0 and not b->v0

                              
  ts, v0
  17:00, 0.5hr
  20:00, 0.5hr

See [Windows and Slices]`ext-hisKit::doc#windowsAndSlices`

hisWrite.name: hisWrite
hisWrite.doc:
Asynchronously write the specified timestamp/value pairs to
the history.  The timestamps must match 'tz' of history.  If
the history has a 'unit' tag, then the items have either a null
or matching unit.  Return future which may be used to track
when write completes - the value of the future subject to change.

Writing data with existing timestamps will replace the current
data with the new data.  Note that timestamp comparison happens
after normalizing timestamps to closest second or millisecond.

The data may be one of the following:
  - Dict with 'ts' and 'val' tags; writes one pair to the history
  - List of Dicts with 'ts' and 'val' tags; writes the list of
    items to the history
  - Grid where first column is 'ts' and second column (may be named
    anything) is the values

The hisRec parameter may be:
  - Ref of history to write to
  - Rec of history to write to

Options:
 - 'noWarn': suppress out of order warning logging
 - 'forecast': set to marker to write as [forecast data]`ext-his::doc#forecast`

Side effects:
  - updates his rec tags hisSize, hisStart, etc
  - clears context read cache

See [documentation]`ext-his::doc#writing` for more details.

instantiate.name: instantiate
instantiate.doc:
Create the default instance for a given spec.
Raise exception if spec is abstract.

The default behavior for dict types is to return a single Dict.
However, if the type has a constrainted query, then an entire graph
can be instantiated via the '{graph}' option in which case a Dict[] is
returned.  In graph mode an 'id' is generated for recs for cross-linking.

Also see `xeto::LibNamespace.instantiate`.

NOTE: this function forces the 'haystack' option to force all
non-Haystack scalars to be simple strings.

Options:
  - 'graph': marker tag to instantiate a graph of recs
  - 'abstract': marker to supress error if spec is abstract

Examples:
                            
  instantiate(Date)

                                                         
  instantiate(G36ReheatVav)

                                                               
  instantiate(G36ReheatVav, {graph})

ioCopy.name: ioCopy
ioCopy.doc:
Copy a file or directory to the new specified location.
If this file represents a directory, then it recursively
copies the entire directory tree.  Both handles must reference
a local file or directory on the file system.

If during the copy, an existing file of the same name is found,
then the "overwrite" option should be to marker or 'true' to
overwrite or 'false' to skip.  Or if overwrite is not defined
then an IOErr is raised.

Examples:
  ioCopy(`io/dir/`, `io/dir-copy/`)
  ioCopy(`io/file.txt`, `io/file-copy.txt`)
  ioCopy(`io/file.txt`, `io/file-copy.txt`, {overwrite})
  ioCopy(`io/file.txt`, `io/file-copy.txt`, {overwrite:false})

ioHttp.name: ioHttp
ioHttp.doc:
Make an HTTP request and process the response in a callback.
The connection is guaranteed to be closed when the callback returns.

The `headers` parameter is an optional Dict of request headers.
Header values may use the special ref [@password] to resolve
a secret from the project's password store.  The password is
looked up by the key "<scheme>://<host>[:<port>]/ <header-name>".

The password key is case sensitive.  If the password is not
found, an exception is raised.

The `body` parameter is any value accepted as an
[I/O handle](doc#handles) (Str, Buf, Uri, etc).  If non-null, it is
streamed as the request body; Content-Type defaults to
"application/octet-stream" when not specified in `headers`.

The callback receives three arguments:
- `code`: Number HTTP status code
- `headers`: Dict of response headers with names normalized to lower-case
- `body`: response body I/O handle for streaming reads

Examples:

// GET and read response as string
ioHttp(`http://example.com/api`, "GET", null, null,
(code, headers, body) => ioReadStr(body))

// POST with body
ioHttp(`http://example.com/api`, "POST",
{"Content-Type": "text/plain"}, "hello world",
(code, headers, body) => {code: code, body: ioReadStr(body)})

// Use password store for auth header
passwordSet("https://acme.com/ Secret-Header", "pass")
ioHttp(`https://acme.com/api`, "POST",
{"Secret-Header": @password}, body,
(code, headers, body) => {code: code, body: ioReadStr(body)})

ioReadCsv.name: ioReadCsv
ioReadCsv.doc:
Read a CSV (comma separated values) file into memory as a Grid.
CSV format is implemented as specified by RFC 4180:
  - rows are delimited by a newline
  - cells are separated by 'delimiter' char
  - cells containing the delimiter, '"' double quote, or
    newline are quoted; quotes are escaped as '""'
  - empty cells are normalized into null

The following options are supported:
  - delimiter: separator char as string, default is ","
  - noHeader: if present then don't treat first row as col names,
    instead use "v0", "v1", etc

Also see `ioStreamCsv`, `ioEachCsv`, `ioWriteCsv`, and `docHaystack::Csv`.

ioReadJson.name: ioReadJson
ioReadJson.doc:
Read a JSON file into memory. This function can used to read any
arbitrary JSON nested object/array structure which can be accessed
as Axon dicts/lists.  The default decoding assumes Haystack 4 JSON
format (Hayson).  Also see `ioReadJsonGrid` if reading a Haystack
formatted grid.

Object keys which are not valid tag names will decode correctly
and can be used in-process.  But they will not serialize correctly
over the HTTP API.  You can use the 'safeNames' option to force object
keys to be safe tag names (but you will lose the original key names).

The following options are supported:
  - v3: decode the JSON as Haystack 3
  - v4: explicitly request Haystack 4 decoding (default)
  - safeNames: convert object keys to safe tag names

ioSkip.name: ioSkip
ioSkip.doc:
Apply a skipping operation to an input I/O handle.  The
following options are available (in order of processing):
  - bom: skip byte order mark
  - bytes: number of bytes to skip (must be binary input stream)
  - chars: number of chars to skip (must be text input stream)
  - lines: number of lines to skip

Skipping a BOM will automatically set the appropiate charset.
If no BOM is detected, then this call is safely ignored by pushing
those bytes back into the input stream.  The following byte
order marks are supported:
  - UTF-16 Big Endian: 0xFE_FF
  - UTF-16 Little Endian: 0xFF_FE
  - UTF-8: 0xEF_BB_BF

Examples:
                                       
  ioSkip(`io/foo.csv`, {lines:4}).ioReadCsv

                         
  ioSkip(`io/foo.csv`, {bom}).ioReadCsv

- bytes: number of bytes to skip (must be binary input stream)
- chars: number of chars to skip (must be text input stream)
- lines: number of lines to skip

Skipping a BOM will automatically set the appropiate charset.
If no BOM is detected, then this call is safely ignored by pushing
those bytes back into the input stream.  The following byte
order marks are supported:
- UTF-16 Big Endian: 0xFE_FF
- UTF-16 Little Endian: 0xFF_FE
- UTF-8: 0xEF_BB_BF

Examples:
// skip leading 4 lines in a CSV file
ioSkip(`io/foo.csv`, {lines:4}).ioReadCsv

// skip byte order mark
ioSkip(`io/foo.csv`, {bom}).ioReadCsv

  - newline: newline string, default is "\n" (use "\r\n" for CRLF)
  - noHeader: Set this option to prevent the column names from being

  - stripUnits: write all numbers without a unit

the visualization:

  - 'text': render as plaintext

  read(power).hisRead(yesterday).ioWritePdf(`io/landscape.pdf`, {pageSize:"11in,8.5in"})

                                         
  readAll(site).ioWritePdf(`io/sites.pdf`, {pageSize:"auto"})

  is(Str, Spec)       >>  true

isMetric.name: isMetric
isMetric.doc:
Given an optional value return true if the SI metric system should be
used.  Return false if the United States customary unit system should be
used.  The following rules are used:
  - if val is a dict with `geoCountry` return return false if "US"
  - if number or rec with `unit` and unit is known to be a US
    customary unit return false (right now we only check
    for °F and Δ°F)
  - fallback to locale of hosting server, see `sys::Locale`

Examples:
   isMetric({geoCountry:"US"})  >>  false
   isMetric({geoCountry:"FR"})  >>  true
   isMetric(75°F)               >>  false
   isMetric({unit:"Δ°C"})       >>  true
   isMetric()                   >>  fallback to server locale
